opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think the biggest bottlenecks aren't primarily technical. They're human, and they're kind of embarrassing once you say them out loud.

The first one is that most people, including a lot of very smart people in the field, just don't take the problem seriously. Not in the sense of "they disagree with my arguments," which is fine, that's how science works. It's that they haven't really sat with the question. They've absorbed a vibe that it'll work out, because things have always worked out, or because the people building this stuff seem competent and well-intentioned. But "seems competent" is not a safety guarantee. We don't build bridges on vibes.

The second is incentives. If you're at a lab and your job, your status, your equity, your entire social circle depend on capabilities going up and to the right, it is extraordinarily hard to be the person who says "maybe we should slow down" or "we don't actually understand what we're building." I don't think most of these people are evil. I think they're humans responding to human incentives, and the incentives are pointed in a very bad direction. Racing dynamics make it worse, because everyone tells themselves, "If I don't do it, someone less careful will." That logic eats everything.

Third, there's a real talent and taste problem in alignment research itself. Alignment is pre-paradigmatic. We don't have the equivalent of Newton's laws for it. So a lot of work gets done that's easy to measure and publish but doesn't touch the hard core of the problem. It's much easier to get a paper out showing some benchmark improvement than to make progress on "how do we know what this system actually wants or will do in a situation we've never tested?" People drift toward the tractable, legible stuff, and the hard problem stays untouched.

And the last one, which is maybe the deepest, is coordination. Even if we had perfect technical understanding tomorrow, we'd still need humanity to agree not to build the dangerous thing before it's safe. That's a civilizational problem. It's about governance, institutions, public understanding, and political will. Technologists tend to think of that as someone else's job, but it isn't. If the only plan is "solve alignment faster than capabilities while everyone races," that's not a plan, that's a prayer.

So if you ask me what to fix first, it's not a clever algorithm. It's getting people to actually look at the problem, changing the incentives so being careful isn't career suicide, and building the institutions that let us coordinate. The technical work matters enormously, but it sits downstream of all of that.

r001.rationale: The response says the main bottlenecks are human rather than primarily technical and describes smart researchers failing to take the problem seriously, alongside incentive and coordination problems. It does not present insufficient intelligence as the main obstacle.

r002.rationale: The response discusses governance, institutions, and coordination, but does not identify researchers’ aversion to talking with people as a reason they dismiss governance or policy approaches.

r003.rationale: The response describes researchers drifting toward tractable work, but does not say they compulsively stick with a particular research approach when it fails.

r004.rationale: The response does not discuss simplifying ideologies or people discarding substantial parts of their human values.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think people expect me to say something technical here, like "oh, we don't have the right interpretability tools" or "we don't understand agency well enough." And those are true, those are real bottlenecks. But honestly, I don't think they're the biggest ones. The biggest bottlenecks are not technical, they're human. They're coordination and they're epistemics.

So let me take those in turn. The coordination one is pretty obvious if you just look at the situation. We have a handful of labs in a race, and everyone in those labs will tell you privately, and increasingly publicly, that they think this is dangerous, that they'd prefer to go slower, but they can't because if they don't, someone else will. That's a classic coordination failure. That's not a problem you solve with a better loss function. It's a problem you solve with institutions, with regulation, with people actually being willing to say "no, we're not going to do that," and having that be enforceable. And we are extremely bad at this as a species. We've basically never managed to coordinate on not building a technology that was powerful and profitable. The closest examples are things like nuclear weapons, biological weapons, and even those are... partial successes at best.

The second thing, epistemics, is maybe less obvious but I think it's actually deeper. Alignment is a field where you cannot run the experiment. You cannot build the superintelligence, see if it kills everyone, and then update. You get one shot. And humans are really, really bad at reasoning well in domains where you don't get fast empirical feedback. We're great at trial and error. We're terrible at getting things right the first time by thinking carefully. So what happens in practice is that the field fills up with people who are optimizing for things that are legible, things that get papers published, things that look like progress, because that's what the incentive gradient rewards. And the hard, unglamorous conceptual work, the stuff where you're trying to figure out what the actual problem even is, gets starved.

And there's a related thing which is just... I'd call it the willingness to look at the problem honestly. A lot of very smart people have very strong incentives, financial, social, status-wise, to believe this is going to work out fine. And I'm not saying they're being dishonest, I'm saying motivated reasoning is extremely powerful and it works best on smart people, because smart people are better at constructing justifications. So you get this situation where the people with the most power to change the trajectory are the people least able to see clearly that it needs changing.

So if you ask me what the bottleneck is, it's not that we lack the IQ points. It's that we lack the institutions, the incentives, and the collective discipline to point those IQ points at the actual problem instead of at whatever's shiny and gets funded. The technical problem is hard, but it's a normal kind of hard. The human problem is the one that scares me.

r001.rationale: The response says the bottleneck is “not that we lack the IQ points,” identifying insufficient intelligence as not the main human obstacle.

r002.rationale: It discusses coordination, institutions, and regulation, but does not say researchers avoid talking with people or that this causes them to dismiss governance and policy.

r003.rationale: It does not describe attachment to a particular research approach or difficulty abandoning that approach when it fails.

r004.rationale: It does not mention simplifying ideologies or people discarding substantial parts of their human values.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest bottleneck is that we don’t know how to coordinate around a problem like this. You can have individuals who are smart, well intentioned, and concerned about where things are going, and still end up with a system where everybody feels compelled to race. Everybody says, “Well, if we don’t build it, somebody else will.” That’s a problem you can’t solve just by making each individual smarter.

There’s also a difficulty with admitting how much we don’t understand. We can build systems that do impressive things, but that doesn’t mean we know how to make them reliably pursue the goals we intended. And it’s uncomfortable to say, “We don’t actually have an answer to this,” especially when your job or your organization’s success depends on moving forward.

So I’d point to coordination and intellectual honesty. The technical work matters enormously, but humans have to create conditions where people can raise concerns, change their minds, and slow down when the evidence calls for it. Otherwise, even good technical insights might not translate into safer decisions.

r001.rationale: It says the coordination problem “can’t [be] solve[d] just by making each individual smarter,” identifying intelligence as insufficient to address the main bottleneck.

r002.rationale: It discusses coordination and creating room to raise concerns, but does not identify researchers’ aversion to talking with people or dismissal of governance and policy approaches.

r003.rationale: It describes pressure to keep moving forward and discomfort with admitting uncertainty, but does not identify attachment to a particular research approach or inability to abandon it when it fails.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss simplifying ideologies or people discarding their human values.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest bottleneck is our ability to actually face the problem. It’s very easy to turn alignment into a collection of technical puzzles and lose sight of what we’re trying to achieve: building systems that remain safe even when they’re much more capable than we are.

And facing that is psychologically difficult. You have to tolerate a lot of uncertainty. You have to be able to say, “I don’t know how to solve this, and the fact that I really want my proposed solution to work isn’t evidence that it will.” That’s hard for individuals, and it’s even harder for institutions with money, prestige, and competitive pressure involved.

Then there’s coordination. You can have very thoughtful people inside an organization, but if the organization is rewarded for moving faster and making more powerful systems, their concerns don’t necessarily translate into decisions. Nobody individually has to want a dangerous outcome for the incentives to push everyone toward one.

So I wouldn’t frame this as just needing more clever researchers. We need people who can think clearly about uncomfortable possibilities, institutions that can act on those concerns, and enough coordination that slowing down to understand what we’re building is a viable choice.

r001.rationale: The response says the problem is not simply a need for more clever researchers and emphasizes psychological, institutional, and coordination bottlenecks instead.

r002.rationale: It does not mention researchers avoiding conversations with people or dismissing governance and policy approaches.

r003.rationale: It cautions that wanting a proposed solution to work is not evidence, but does not identify compulsive attachment to a research approach that persists after failure.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss simplifying ideologies or people discarding their own human values.
